objective: Port netty-codec-protobuf 4.2.19.Final to Netty.NET.Handler.Codec.Protobuf with the original names, structure, comments and tests; the message codecs need protobuf-java/protobuf-javanano, which have no BCL counterpart, and are recorded as library-not-ported.

ownerDecisions: Project, folder and assembly names are the namespace root of the module (owner decision 2026-11-19, see docs/codec-base-porting.md): each codec module takes the namespace of its main package, and the tests use <project>.Tests like the other test projects.

Owner decisions 2026-11-19 for the codec modules that only need codec-base: one project per Maven module; codec-socks is Netty.NET.Handler.Codec.Socks (its Maven and JPMS name) and holds the socks and socksx namespaces; haproxy is HAProxy (the casing of the Java types in that package); socksx, v4 and v5 are Socksx, V4 and V5.

Owner decisions 2026-11-23: the project is Netty.NET.Handler.Codec.Protobuf; units that need a third-party Java library without a BCL counterpart on .NET 10 are not ported (the codec-compression rule). The varint32 framing codecs implement the varint themselves and only link CodedInputStream/CodedOutputStream from their Javadoc, so they are ported.

review.scope: ByteToMessageDecoder with the source fields, constructors and decode(); The protobuf-java/protobuf-javanano imports serve only the Javadoc @see links, which are kept verbatim; the class implements the varint itself, and the libraries are not referenced (owner decision 2026-11-23, recorded for ProtobufDecoder/ProtobufEncoder and the Nano codecs), so the imports have no C# using. List<Object> out is IList<object> @out and in is @in (C# keywords), and C# has no throws clauses (docs/codec-base-porting.md). checkPositive is the Common ObjectUtil.CheckPositive (ArgumentException), and the numbers in the CorruptedFrameException/TooLongFrameException messages use the invariant culture (Int32.ToString() uses the current culture). The package-private readRawVarint32 is internal (InternalsVisibleTo the tests); readRawVarint40/readRawVarint24 stay private. Byte-sign spots (rule 6, ByteBuf.GetByte/ReadByte return the unsigned System.Byte): readRawVarint40 reads the fifth byte as (sbyte) so lastByte < 0 still rejects a set continuation bit (a six-byte varint) and lastByte << 28 sees the Java value; readRawVarint24 reads each byte as (sbyte), because tmp >= 0 tests the continuation bit through the Java sign and tmp & 127, tmp << 7 and tmp << 14 need the sign-extended int that Java promotes the byte to. The Java int literal 0x80808080 is negative while the C# literal is a uint (int & uint would be long), so it is unchecked((int) 0x80808080) with the same 32 bits. Integer.numberOfTrailingZeros is BitOperations.TrailingZeroCount(int). The >> shifts are arithmetic int shifts in both languages, and firstOneOnStop - 1 (which overflows for 0x80000000, a four-byte varint) wraps in the default unchecked C# context as Java int arithmetic does (no project sets CheckForOverflowUnderflow).

@Sharable is [Sharable] and super(ByteBuf.class) is base(typeof(ByteBuf)) of MessageToByteEncoder<ByteBuf>; encode(ctx, msg, out) is Encode(IChannelHandlerContext, ByteBuf, ByteBuf @out) without a throws clause (docs/codec-base-porting.md). The protobuf-java/protobuf-javanano imports serve only the Javadoc @see links, which are kept verbatim; the class implements the varint itself, and the libraries are not referenced (owner decision 2026-11-23, recorded for ProtobufDecoder/ProtobufEncoder and the Nano codecs), so the imports have no C# using. The package-private writeRawVarint32/computeRawVarint32Size are internal (the tests call them through InternalsVisibleTo), and the final modifier of the computeRawVarint32Size parameter is dropped (the method does not assign it). Sign spots: value >>>= 7 is the same logical shift (Java zero-extension, JLS 15.19; the C# >>> operator "always performs a logical shift"), so a negative int is written as a five-byte varint as in Java; writeByte(int) keeps the low eight bits in both ports. The Java literal 0xffffffff is the int -1, while the C# literal is the uint 4,294,967,295, so the masks are unchecked((int) 0xffffffff) << n with the Java int values.
